section.title: The Samaritan Woman and the Official's Son
section.sectionRationale: From a learned Pharisee by night the Gospel turns to a Samaritan woman at noon, an outsider by race, gender, and reputation. Jesus crosses every barrier to offer her living water and to reveal Himself as the Messiah, and she becomes an evangelist to her town. The chapter closes with the second sign, the healing of an official's son at a distance, a man who simply takes Jesus at His word.
section.thesis: Jesus freely crosses the barriers of race, gender, and shame to give living water that becomes a spring of eternal life, revealing Himself as the Christ and the Savior of the world whom the Father seeks worshipers to worship in spirit and truth, and He is trusted at His bare word by an official whose son He heals from afar.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the request for a drink and the offer of living water; true worship in spirit and truth and Jesus' self-revelation as Messiah; the woman's witness and the Samaritans' faith in the Savior of the world; and the healing of the official's son, the second sign, received by faith in Jesus' word.

units.label: Living water at the well
units.note: a spring welling up to eternal life

verses.text: When Jesus realized that the Pharisees were aware He was gaining and baptizing more disciples than John
(although it was not Jesus who baptized, but His disciples),
He left Judea and returned to Galilee.
Now He had to pass through Samaria.
So He came to a town of Samaria called Sychar, near the plot of ground that Jacob had given to his son Joseph.
Since Jacob’s well was there, Jesus, weary from His journey, sat down by the well. It was about the sixth hour.
When a Samaritan woman came to draw water, Jesus said to her, “Give Me a drink.”
(His disciples had gone into the town to buy food.)
“You are a Jew,” said the woman. “How can You ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?” (For Jews do not associate with Samaritans.)
Jesus answered, “If you knew the gift of God and who is asking you for a drink, you would have asked Him, and He would have given you {{hydorzon|living water}}.”
“Sir,” the woman replied, “You have nothing to draw with and the well is deep. Where then will You get this living water?
Are You greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well and drank from it himself, as did his sons and his livestock?”
Jesus said to her, “Everyone who drinks this water will be thirsty again.
But whoever drinks the water I give him will never thirst. Indeed, the water I give him will become in him a fount of water springing up to eternal life.”
The woman said to Him, “Sir, give me this water so that I will not get thirsty and have to keep coming here to draw water.”
Jesus told her, “Go, call your husband and come back.”
“I have no husband,” the woman replied. Jesus said to her, “You are correct to say that you have no husband.
In fact, you have had five husbands, and the man you now have is not your husband. You have spoken truthfully.”
“Sir,” the woman said, “I see that You are a prophet.
Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you Jews say that the place where one must worship is in Jerusalem.”
“Believe Me, woman,” Jesus replied, “a time is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.
You worship what you do not know; we worship what we do know, for salvation is from the Jews.
But a time is coming and has now come when the true worshipers will worship the Father in {{pneuma|spirit}} and in truth, for the Father is seeking such as these to worship Him.
God is Spirit, and His worshipers must worship Him in spirit and in truth.”
The woman said, “I know that Messiah” (called Christ) “is coming. When He comes, He will explain everything to us.”
Jesus answered, “I who speak to you {{egoeimi|am He}}.”

units.label: The woman's witness and the Samaritans' faith

verses.text: Just then His disciples returned and were surprised that He was speaking with a woman. But no one asked Him, “What do You want from her?” or “Why are You talking with her?”
Then the woman left her water jar, went back into the town, and said to the people,
“Come, see a man who told me everything I ever did. Could this be the Christ?”
So they left the town and made their way toward Jesus.
Meanwhile the disciples urged Him, “Rabbi, eat something.”
But He told them, “I have food to eat that you know nothing about.”
So the disciples asked one another, “Could someone have brought Him food?”
Jesus explained, “My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me and to finish His work.
Do you not say, ‘There are still four months until the harvest’? I tell you, lift up your eyes and look at the fields, for they are ripe for harvest.
Already the reaper draws his wages and gathers a crop for eternal life, so that the sower and the reaper may rejoice together.
For in this case the saying ‘One sows and another reaps’ is true.
I sent you to reap what you have not worked for; others have done the hard work, and now you have taken up their labor.”
Many of the Samaritans from that town believed in Jesus because of the woman’s testimony, “He told me everything I ever did.”
So when the Samaritans came to Him, they asked Him to stay with them, and He stayed two days.
And many more believed because of His message.
They said to the woman, “We now believe not only because of your words; we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this man truly is the {{soter|Savior}} of the world.”

units.label: The official's son healed
units.note: the second sign, faith in the word

verses.text: After two days, Jesus left for Galilee.
Now He Himself had testified that a prophet has no honor in his own hometown.
Yet when He arrived, the Galileans welcomed Him. They had seen all the great things He had done in Jerusalem at the feast, for they had gone there as well.
So once again He came to Cana in Galilee, where He had turned the water into wine. And there was a royal official whose son lay sick at Capernaum.
When he heard that Jesus had come from Judea to Galilee, he went and begged Him to come down and heal his son, who was about to die.
Jesus said to him, “Unless you people see signs and wonders, you will never believe.”
“Sir,” the official said, “come down before my child dies.”
“Go,” said Jesus. “Your son will live.” The man took Jesus at His word and departed.
And while he was still on the way, his servants met him with the news that his boy was alive.
So he inquired as to the hour when his son had recovered, and they told him, “The fever left him yesterday at the seventh hour.”
Then the father realized that this was the very hour in which Jesus had told him, “Your son will live.” And he and all his household believed.
This was now the second sign that Jesus performed after coming from Judea into Galilee.

hydorzon.gloss: Living water. The phrase ordinarily meant fresh, flowing water rather than still cistern water, and the woman first hears it that way. Jesus means something greater: the gift of God, the life He gives by the Spirit, which becomes an inner spring welling up to eternal life. It answers a thirst that Jacob's well never could.

pneuma.gloss: Spirit. God is Spirit, and true worship is offered in spirit and in truth, not bound to a particular mountain or temple. The word points to worship that is inward and real, made possible by the Holy Spirit, the same Spirit Jesus links to the living water and the new birth. Place gives way to the Spirit and the truth who is Christ.

egoeimi.gloss: I am, or I am He. To the woman's expectation of Messiah, Jesus answers literally I am, the phrase that in John repeatedly echoes the divine name revealed to Moses, I AM. It is His plainest self-disclosure so far, given not to a scholar in Jerusalem but to a Samaritan woman at a well, and it anticipates the great I am sayings to come.

soter.gloss: Savior, deliverer, rescuer. The Samaritans confess Jesus as the Savior of the world, a title that in the Roman world was claimed by Caesar. John records outsiders grasping what many insiders miss: that Jesus saves not one nation only but the world, exactly the reach of God's love in giving His Son.

basic.context: Jesus takes the road through Samaria, land the Jews avoided, and rests at Jacob's well at noon. A Samaritan woman comes to draw water, and Jesus, crossing every social line, asks her for a drink and offers her living water. He gently exposes her broken past, and she raises the old dispute about where to worship. Jesus lifts worship above places to spirit and truth, then reveals plainly that He is the Messiah. She runs to tell her town, and many believe. The chapter ends with a royal official who simply trusts Jesus' word, Your son will live, and finds it so.
basic.hermeneutics: Watch how Jesus moves from a physical thing, water, to a spiritual reality, the life He gives, a pattern all through John. The key questions are, what is the living water, what is true worship, and what does faith look like. The answers: the living water is the Spirit and the life Jesus gives; true worship is in spirit and truth, centered on Christ; and faith takes Jesus at His word, as the official did, without needing to see first.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter turns on a few key terms. Jesus offers hydor zon, living water, that becomes a spring of eternal life. He teaches worship in pneuma, spirit, and truth, for God is Spirit. To the woman He says ego eimi, I am He, the divine self-disclosure. And the Samaritans confess Him soter, the Savior of the world.
basic.typology: Jacob's well, given by the patriarch, is surpassed by the water Jesus gives; the meeting at a well, where Isaac and Jacob found brides, hints at the bridegroom gathering His people. The harvest imagery gathers the ingathering of the nations that the prophets foresaw.
basic.christ: Christ reveals Himself as the giver of living water, the one greater than Jacob, the Messiah who tells all things, and the Savior of the world. He is trusted at His bare word by the official, and His word carries the power to give life at a distance.
basic.god: God is Spirit, and He is seeking worshipers, actively looking for people to draw near in spirit and truth. Salvation is from the Jews, yet God's reach is the whole world. The Father sends the Son, whose very food is to do His will and finish His work.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 55 invites the thirsty to come to the waters. Jeremiah 2 contrasts the fountain of living water with broken cisterns. John 7 unfolds the living water as the Spirit. 1 John 4 confesses the Son as the Savior of the world.
basic.oneStory: The gift of living water and the offer of true worship reach beyond Israel to a Samaritan outsider and her town, a first fruits of the nations. Jesus, greater than Jacob, is the Messiah and Savior of the world, and the harvest of all peoples that the prophets foresaw has begun to be gathered to Him.

context.literary:
Chapter 4 reads as a diptych bracketed by Cana. It begins with Jesus leaving Judea and ends with His return 'once again' to Cana in Galilee, verse 46, so that the second sign of verse 54 closes a frame opened by the first at 2:11. Between those two points lie two very different people: a woman of no name at noon, and a royal official of rank at the seventh hour. One is an outsider by race and reputation, the other an insider by position, and both come to Jesus in need and leave believing. Faith in this chapter has no social type.

The long dialogue at the well is a ladder of rising recognition. The woman first sees 'a Jew,' verse 9; then 'Sir,' verse 11; then asks if He is greater than Jacob, verse 12; then 'a prophet,' verse 19; then wonders aloud whether He might be the Christ, verse 29; and the townspeople finally say 'Savior of the world,' verse 42. Each step is a response to something Jesus has said or known. John makes the movement of her understanding the structure of the scene.

The writing leans on misunderstanding, as in chapter 3. Jesus speaks of living water and she thinks of a bucket and a rope. Jesus speaks of food and the disciples think of a lunch. Each time the physical thing is real, and the spiritual thing is realer. The disciples' return in verse 27 divides the scene in two and creates a deliberate pause: their puzzlement is silent, and the woman's departure at that moment carries its own meaning, since she leaves her water jar. The story of her witness runs in parallel with the disciples' lesson about harvest, so that while the men talk about food the town is already walking out to the field.

Finally, the chapter has a refrain in the form of small repeated words. 'Come, see' in verse 29 echoes chapter 1, 'stay' in verse 40 uses the verb of abiding, and in the official's story the key word 'lives' sounds three times, in verses 50, 51 and 53, like a bell.
context.historical:
The Samaritans were the people of the old northern kingdom's region, centered on Shechem and Mount Gerizim. After Assyria took Israel into exile, foreign settlers were brought in, and 2 Kings 17:24-41 describes a mixed worship that Jews remembered with suspicion. The Samaritans, for their part, kept the Torah, claimed descent from Joseph's tribes, and held Mount Gerizim, not Jerusalem, to be the place God had chosen. Their temple on Gerizim was destroyed by the Hasmonean ruler John Hyrcanus in the second century BC, as Josephus reports, which left a long memory of injury. The mountain 'this mountain' of verse 20 was in plain sight of the well.

The setting itself is loaded with patriarchal memory. Jacob bought land near Shechem, Genesis 33:19, and Joseph's bones were later buried there, Joshua 24:32, which is why the text recalls the plot that Jacob had given to Joseph. The well is not mentioned in the Old Testament, but local tradition tied it to Jacob. The route through Samaria was the shortest way from Judea to Galilee, and Josephus says that Galilean pilgrims often took it, though many Jews avoided the region, so the 'had to' of verse 4 may be geographical or may be divine necessity.

Noon was not the time women usually drew water, which suggests that this woman came when she would meet no one. A Jewish teacher speaking alone with a woman, and a Samaritan, was out of the ordinary in the extreme, and the disciples' surprise in verse 27 reflects the custom. The remark in verse 9 that Jews do not associate with Samaritans uses a verb that probably means sharing things in common, such as vessels, which gives the request for a drink its edge.

Samaritans accepted the five books of Moses and looked for a coming prophet like Moses, from Deuteronomy 18. The woman's reference to a Messiah who will 'explain everything' fits that expectation. In the second half, the royal official was a man in the service of the ruler of Galilee, probably Herod Antipas, and Capernaum lay about a day's journey from Cana. The time marks, the seventh hour and 'yesterday,' fit a walk home that took a full day.
context.canonical:
The scene at the well belongs to a clear Old Testament pattern. Betrothal stories happen at wells: Abraham's servant meets Rebekah, Genesis 24:11-20; Jacob meets Rachel, Genesis 29:1-12; Moses meets Zipporah, Exodus 2:15-21. A traveler sits by a well, a woman comes to draw, water is given, and a household is joined. John does not make the parallel explicit, but a reader of Genesis would feel the outlines, and the Baptist has just called Jesus the bridegroom in 3:29. The twist is that this woman is drawn to a different kind of union, with a man who will not marry her but will give her life.

Water is also the prophets' picture of God's gift. Jeremiah 2:13 says that Israel forsook 'the fountain of living water' and dug broken cisterns. Isaiah 55:1 invites everyone who is thirsty to come to the waters. Isaiah 12:3 speaks of drawing water with joy from the wells of salvation, Isaiah 44:3 pairs water with the outpouring of God's Spirit, and Zechariah 14:8 says that living water will flow out from Jerusalem. Ezekiel 47 sees a river flowing from the temple. John unfolds the image later: in John 7:37-39 Jesus cries that whoever believes will have streams of living water flowing from within, and the narrator says that He meant the Spirit.

The argument about worship has deep roots in the question of the chosen place. Deuteronomy 12 speaks of the place the LORD would choose, and Solomon's prayer at the dedication, 1 Kings 8, imagines God's name dwelling there. Isaiah 2:3 and Malachi 1:11 look to a day when the nations will worship. Jesus' words 'spirit and truth' also anticipate Paul's phrase about worshiping by the Spirit of God, Philippians 3:3, and Hebrews 8 and 9 on a true tabernacle.

The harvest sayings draw on Joel 3:13 and Amos 9:13 and are repeated in Matthew 9:37-38. And the confession 'Savior of the world' recurs in 1 John 4:14, which states in nearly the same words that the Father has sent His Son to be the Savior of the world, while the theme of faith by word alone is echoed in Jesus' blessing of those who believe without seeing, John 20:29.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John pairs the woman and the official to show that Jesus reaches across every boundary the first readers might have assumed. The woman is a Samaritan, a woman, and a person with a complicated past; the official is a man of rank, a Gentile or a Jew in the pay of the court. By including them both, John tells readers that the Savior of the world has no waiting-list. The Gospel's first-century audience, which included Samaritans and Gentiles as well as Jews, was meant to see itself in these stories.

He also wants the reader to feel the gentleness of Jesus' way. He asks for a drink before He offers one. He names her life without condemning her, and in that exposure she finds she is known, not rejected, which is why she tells the town. John presents a Jesus who is neither softer nor harsher than the truth, who tells the truth and offers living water in the same conversation.

Finally the chapter has a missionary purpose. The disciples are called to look up from their lunch and see fields ready for harvest, and the example of the woman is placed before them. A person with a shaky reputation and no training becomes the instrument of a town's faith. The author invites readers to value testimony that is simple and true: 'He told me everything I ever did,' and then to move on to the faith that comes by hearing Him for oneself.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes how one woman and one household came to faith, and it records that Jesus knew her history. It does not prescribe confronting people with their past as a method of evangelism, nor does it set up the five husbands as a template for diagnosing sin. Jesus speaks as the one who knows the heart, which is something no disciple can imitate, and the story shows grace rather than a technique.

What the chapter does model is worth keeping. Jesus crosses boundaries of race, gender and reputation to speak with a person. He starts with something ordinary, a drink of water, and moves to something deep. He answers her side-issue about the mountain but does not let it replace her need. And He welcomes the testimony of someone with an imperfect past, then lets the town hear Him for themselves.

On worship, the passage is descriptive of a coming change that has already begun with Him, and it prescribes the character of worship, which is spirit and truth, not a particular location. That does not make gathered worship optional elsewhere in Scripture, and it does not abolish forms. It says that no place, whether Gerizim or Jerusalem or a particular building, is the guarantee of being heard. The official's story prescribes nothing but trust: he went home on the strength of a word, as believers still do.

debates.question: What are the five husbands and the man who is not her husband about?

views.label: A literal history that Jesus knew supernaturally
views.case: The text says 'you have had five husbands, and the man you now have is not your husband,' and the woman responds, 'I see that You are a prophet.' Later she tells the town that He told her everything she ever did. The plain sense is that Jesus revealed what no stranger could know.

views.label: A symbolic reference to Samaria's history
views.case: After Assyria resettled the land, five peoples brought their gods to Samaria, 2 Kings 17:24-34, and the LORD is spoken of as a husband of Israel, Hosea 2:16. On this view the five husbands are a figure of Samaria's mixed worship, and the sixth, not a husband, is the illegitimate worship that Jesus is about to correct.

views.label: Both at once
views.case: The conversation turns on her real history, and the same pattern of divided loyalty haunts her people. Some hold that John's Gospel works in just this double way, so that a real life becomes a window onto a wider truth.

debates.bearing: The literal sense is secure, since the woman herself takes it so. A symbolic overlay is possible but not demanded, and it is better held loosely. The story's force lies in the fact that He knows and still offers the gift.

debates.question: What does worship 'in spirit and in truth' mean?

views.label: In the Holy Spirit and in the truth that is Christ
views.case: John presents the Spirit as the one who gives life and the Spirit of truth, John 14:17 and 16:13, and Jesus as the truth, John 14:6. So worship is enabled by the Spirit and centered on the Son, which is what the passage's movement from place to person suggests.

views.label: Inwardly and sincerely, as opposed to external rites
views.case: Spirit refers to the human spirit and truth to sincerity, in contrast with ritual alone. This echoes prophets who said God desires the heart, Psalm 51:16-17, and it fits God's nature as Spirit, verse 24.

views.label: With the true object, in the new age
views.case: Truth here means the reality that has now arrived, as opposed to Samaritan ignorance and Jewish shadow. The emphasis is on the fulfillment in Christ, in line with verse 22, 'salvation is from the Jews,' and with John 1:17.

debates.bearing: These readings overlap, and most careful interpreters combine the first and third. In every case the verse removes worship from a geography and places it in a relationship made possible by the Spirit through the Son.

debates.question: What does verse 44 mean by a prophet having no honor in his own hometown?

views.label: His own country is Galilee
views.case: Verse 45 says the Galileans welcomed Him, which makes it odd if 'his own country' were Galilee. Still, Nazareth is in Galilee, and the welcome was an enthusiasm based on wonders, not real honor, as verse 48 hints.

views.label: His own country is Judea
views.case: Jesus left Judea at the beginning of the chapter, and in the Gospel He is rejected in Jerusalem. On this view the saying explains His departure from there and His going to Galilee, where the welcome came because they had seen what He did at the feast.

debates.bearing: Both readings account for the awkward 'for' of verse 44. What matters for the story is that a welcome based on signs is not the same as faith, and the official's trust in a bare word is the contrast.

study.originalLanguages:
Start with the two words for the source of water. In verse 6 John calls Jacob's well a pege, a spring, but in verses 11 and 12 the woman calls it a phrear, a deep shaft or cistern. In verse 14 Jesus says the water He gives will be a pege, a spring, which is the same word. The woman talks of a pit that needs a bucket, while Jesus speaks of a spring that flows from inside a person. The difference between a cistern and a spring is the difference Jeremiah drew in 2:13.

'Living water,' hydor zon, was an ordinary phrase for flowing water as opposed to still, stored water, found in Genesis 26:19 of Isaac's servants digging and finding a well of springing water. That ambiguity is the hinge of the misunderstanding: the woman hears 'running water' and Jesus means life itself. In verse 14 the water becomes in a person a spring 'springing up,' using the verb hallomai, which is the verb for leaping, used in Acts 3:8 of the lame man who jumped up. The image is not of a still well but of water that bounds upward. It is described as 'to eternal life,' the same phrase as in 3:15 and 3:16.

Third, notice 'I am He' in verse 26. The Greek is ego eimi, with the clause 'the one speaking to you.' In this place it is a plain statement that He is the Messiah of whom she has spoken. Yet the wording is close to the Greek of Isaiah 52:6, where the LORD says that His people will know that He is the one speaking, which gives the phrase an overtone of divine self-disclosure. John uses the same two words in later chapters in ways that more clearly claim the divine name, as in John 8:58.

Fourth, the verb 'worship,' proskuneo, which means to bow down or to kneel, appears again and again in verses 20 to 24, and the repeated 'must' of verse 24 says that this is the way worship has to be. The word 'truth,' aletheia, is one of John's key words, the reality revealed in Christ, and 'seeking' in verse 23 shows that the Father is the one who initiates. Notice also the word translated 'such as these' that identifies a kind of person whom the Father looks for.

Fifth, 'Savior of the world,' soter tou kosmou, in verse 42. The title appears in the New Testament here and in 1 John 4:14. It was a title also applied to rulers in the Greek world, and the Samaritans' use of it for a Jewish teacher carries a double edge. 'The world' stretches the term beyond Jew and Samaritan. Finally, the verb 'stay' in verse 40 is meno, the Gospel's word for abiding, and the people who asked Him to stay received the kind of fellowship that the first disciples had in 1:39.

typology.type: The well and the betrothal scenes, Genesis 24, Genesis 29 and Exodus 2
typology.fulfillment: Three patriarchal stories have a man at a well, a woman who comes to draw, water given and a household formed. John 4 echoes the pattern and then turns it. Jesus sits at the well, the woman comes, but it is He who asks for water and then offers it, and the union He seeks is faith. The Baptist has just called Jesus the bridegroom, John 3:29, and the prophets speak of God betrothing His people, Hosea 2:19-20. The escalation is from an individual marriage to the gathering of a whole people, as the town comes out. The type falls short in that no marriage is made here at all; John does not push the allusion beyond a quiet suggestion, and we should not either.

typology.type: Jacob's well and the patriarch's gift
typology.fulfillment: The woman asks whether Jesus is greater than Jacob, who gave the well and drank from it with his sons and flocks. Jacob stands for the whole inheritance of the fathers, and he provided water that left people thirsty again. Jesus provides water that becomes a spring. The correspondence is that both are givers of water, and the escalation is that the water of Jesus is eternal and internal. Jacob also saw heaven opened at Bethel, which Jesus took to Himself in John 1:51. The type falls short in that the well was a real good and a real provision, and the text does not mock it.

typology.type: The ripe fields and the harvest
typology.fulfillment: The Old Testament pictures the ingathering of nations as a harvest, Joel 3:13, and speaks of a day when the plowman overtakes the reaper, Amos 9:13. Jesus tells the disciples to look up at fields ready now, and He points to a Samaritan crowd walking out of the town. The sower and the reaper rejoice together. The escalation is that the age of harvest has begun with Him, and its workers enter into labor that others have done, the prophets and John among them. The type falls short in that the harvest here is only a first fruit, and the end of the age still lies ahead, Matthew 13:39.

typology.type: The water of the Spirit from the temple, Ezekiel 47 and Zechariah 14:8
typology.fulfillment: The prophets saw a river flowing from the house of God, bringing life wherever it went. Jesus offers a spring within a person, and in John 7:38-39 the narrator says the Spirit is meant. The correspondence is of living water flowing from God's presence. The escalation is that the source moves from a building to a person, and then to those who believe in Him. The type falls short in that Ezekiel's river flows from a future temple, whereas the Gospel reports water already at hand to a thirsty woman in Samaria.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ through His own self-disclosures, and each one is an answer to a question that the woman or the Old Testament had left open.

She asks whether He is greater than Jacob, and the answer comes in the whole conversation. Jacob dug or inherited a well; Jesus gives a spring. Jacob's gift was drunk from and drunk again; Jesus' gift quenches for good. Jesus is the Son who gives the Spirit, and the narrator in 7:39 says so. Jeremiah accused Israel of forsaking the fountain of living water, and when Jesus offers it, He presents Himself as that fountain's giver. What the LORD claimed to be in the prophets, Jesus offers as His own to give.

She says the Messiah will explain everything, and He answers 'I am He.' This is the plainest statement of His identity in the first half of the Gospel, and He makes it to a Samaritan woman, not to the leaders in Jerusalem. The first named recipient of the full disclosure is an outsider with a past. The saying that salvation is from the Jews puts Him firmly in Israel's story, and the saying that the Father seeks worshipers puts Him at the center of a new age. He is the one in whom worship in spirit and truth becomes possible, being Himself the truth, John 14:6, and the giver of the Spirit.

He is also the one who finishes the Father's work. 'My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me and to finish His work,' verse 34, anticipates the cry from the cross, 'It is finished,' John 19:30, from the same family of words about completion. Fatigue and thirst, verses 6 and 7, are real human conditions, so He who asks for a drink is the Word made flesh. He gets tired, and yet He is never short of what He came to do.

Finally, He is the Savior of the world. The Samaritans' confession in verse 42 reaches beyond the boundaries of Israel and sets Jesus as the answer to the promises that all nations would be blessed. The official's story adds that His word is enough, even at a distance. The one who made the water wine and the one who gave life to a dying boy are the same, and His word carries creative power, as in Psalm 107:20, 'He sent forth His word and healed them.' 

A word of care. The jar left at the well, the sixth hour, and the five husbands are not secret codes. Where the text makes a link, we follow it: the spring, the Spirit, the harvest, the Savior of the world. Where it does not, it is better to enjoy the detail as the story's own texture.
study.god:
The chapter's central statement about God is that He is Spirit, verse 24, and the whole argument about worship follows from it. A God who is Spirit is not limited to a mountain or a city. He cannot be located in a building, and He cannot be managed by a ritual. The statement is not a denial that God is personal, for the same verse says He seeks worshipers. It is a statement that His presence is not confined, so that the fitting response is not geography but relationship.

He is a God who seeks. The Father is 'seeking such as these to worship Him,' verse 23, so the initiative lies with Him. In the story, Jesus sits down at a well and waits for a woman who has come at noon to avoid being seen. The Gospel makes the point again in the order of the story: the one who asks for a drink is the one who gives, and the seeker is the sought. That is a great comfort in a world that thinks of religion as a human quest.

God is a God of truth, who will not pretend. Jesus names the woman's history plainly, and the grace of the chapter is not found in ignoring facts but in meeting them. His holiness does not hide away from her. The same God who knows everything she ever did offers her a gift she did not earn. That joins justice and mercy in one scene, and teaches that to be known by Him is the beginning of being healed.

He is also the God of the whole world. The Samaritan confession of 'Savior of the world' stands in line with the promise to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed, Genesis 12:3, and the saying that salvation is from the Jews keeps that promise rooted in history. God does not choose between particularity and universality; He works through a particular people to bless every people. And He is a God whose word is effective. The official's boy lives at the very hour that Jesus speaks, and the word has no need of presence.

For worship, this means a few concrete things. We need not travel to a holy place to be heard. We worship in the Spirit whom the Son gives and in the truth who is the Son. We come as those who are known and already sought. And we can expect that when the Father seeks, He finds people from unlikely places, as He found a woman at a well, a town that asked Him to stay, and a household that believed on a promise it could not yet see.

crossReferences.note: God accuses His people of forsaking the fountain of living water and digging broken cisterns that cannot hold water. The woman's well is a cistern, and Jesus offers the fountain, so the whole exchange can be read as God's old complaint answered by a gift: the source Israel left has come looking for a thirsty person.

Everyone who is thirsty is invited to come to the waters, even those without money. Jesus' offer to a woman who has nothing to pay and no standing is the fulfillment of this open invitation, and it shows that the gift is free to anyone who is willing to ask.

On the coming day living water flows out from Jerusalem in summer and winter alike. The picture of an unfailing supply sits behind Jesus' claim that those who drink will never thirst, and it also shows that the source in the prophets is God's own presence.

On the last day of the feast Jesus calls the thirsty to come and drink, and says that streams of living water will flow from within the believer. The narrator explains that He meant the Spirit, which tells us how to read the water of John 4, a gift given after He is glorified.

Abraham's servant meets Rebekah at a well, where she draws water for him and his camels. The sequence of a traveler, a woman at the well and an act of drawing water is the pattern that the reader is meant to recall, and Jesus' reversal of it, asking for a drink to give a better one, shows what is new.

Jacob buys a piece of land near Shechem, the place where the Samaritan woman's town now stood. The history of the plot gives the woman's question about Jacob its weight, since she is speaking from within an inheritance that Jesus claims to outdo.

The king of Assyria brings people from other lands to settle in the cities of Samaria. The passage explains the mixed origin of the Samaritans and the long distrust between them and the Jews, which gives the surprise of verse 9 and the disciples' astonishment in verse 27 their background.

The plowman overtakes the reaper and the sower overtakes the one treading grapes. This promise of a harvest so abundant that the seasons run together matches Jesus' words that sower and reaper rejoice together, and it suggests that a long awaited age has begun.

God sent out His word and healed them and delivered them from the grave. The official's boy lives because of a word spoken twenty miles away, and the psalm shows that the Old Testament already ascribed this power to God's word, which the Gospel here places in Jesus' mouth.

John writes that the Father has sent the Son to be the Savior of the world. The phrase uses the Samaritans' confession of verse 42 almost exactly, so the apostle later states in his own voice what the first outsiders believed at the well.

Jesus blesses those who have not seen and yet have believed. The royal official, who took Jesus at His word and set off before any sign, is an early example of this blessing, and the Gospel uses his story to prepare readers who will never see the signs for themselves.

study.oneStory:
From the beginning of the Bible, water means life. Eden had a river, Genesis 2:10, and the patriarchs' wanderings turn on wells. The prophets then used water to describe what Israel had lost and what God would restore: a fountain forsaken, a river from the temple, a thirst that only God could satisfy. At the same time the story had a deep division. The kingdom split, the north fell, and the region of Samaria became a people regarded as both kin and stranger. The question of where to worship and who belonged to God ran like a fault line through the Old Testament world.

This chapter takes up both strands. In a place of old wounds, between Jew and Samaritan, Jesus offers the water that the prophets had longed for and ends the dispute about the place of worship by pointing to a person and a Spirit. It answers the question left by the exile: how will the scattered and the estranged be gathered? Not by returning to the old boundaries but by a harvest of those who believe. And it answers the question left by Genesis 12: how will the nations be blessed? One by one, beginning with a woman at a well.

It sets up the rest of the Bible's story. The Gospel will carry the offer of living water to the crowds at the feast, John 7, and the risen Christ will send His disciples to Samaria in particular, Acts 1:8. Acts 8 records Philip going down to a city in Samaria, where people receive the word and the Spirit, so the harvest begun in John 4 is brought in. The official and his household anticipate the households that believe in Acts, such as Cornelius's and the Philippian jailer's.

The story ends with water and worship in a new creation. The river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, Revelation 22:1, the Spirit and the bride say 'Come,' and the one who is thirsty is invited to take the water of life freely, Revelation 22:17. The nations are healed, and there is no more temple on a mountain, for the Lord God and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22. The woman who left her jar at the well would recognize what is offered there, because it is what she was first offered at noon.

quiz.q: What is the living water Jesus offers the Samaritan woman?

options.text: The gift of God, the life of the Spirit that becomes an inner spring welling up to eternal life.
options.note: Verses 10 and 14 describe a gift that satisfies forever and springs up to eternal life, later named as the Spirit in John 7.

options.text: Fresh flowing spring water rather than well water.
options.note: This is how the woman first hears it, but Jesus means the spiritual gift of eternal life, not literal water.

options.text: The eternal life and salvation Jesus gives.
options.note: True and close, but it does not name the Spirit and the inner spring that the passage and John 7 specify.

options.text: The water of Jacob's well, blessed for the patriarchs.
options.note: Jesus contrasts His water with Jacob's well, which leaves people thirsty again.

quiz.q: What does Jesus teach about true worship?

options.text: True worshipers worship the Father in spirit and in truth, for God is Spirit.
options.note: Verses 23 and 24 lift worship above any sacred location to spirit and truth.

options.text: Worship must happen only in Jerusalem, as the Jews said.
options.note: Jesus affirms salvation is from the Jews, but says a time has come when worship is bound to no place.

options.text: Worship is no longer tied to a mountain or temple but to the Father.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but it omits the heart of Jesus' teaching, worship in spirit and truth.

options.text: Any sincere worship of any god is acceptable.
options.note: Jesus ties true worship to the truth and to knowing the Father; not all worship is the same.

quiz.q: How does Jesus reveal His identity to the woman?

options.text: He plainly says I who speak to you am He, the Messiah.
options.note: Verse 26 records His direct self-disclosure as the Christ, using the words I am He.

options.text: He performs a miracle to prove who He is.
options.note: He reveals Himself by word, not by a miracle in this scene.

options.text: He tells her the history of her life, showing prophetic insight.
options.note: He does show supernatural knowledge, which leads her to call Him a prophet, but the climactic revelation is His own claim, I am He.

options.text: He lets her guess and never confirms it.
options.note: He does not leave it to guessing; He openly confirms He is the Messiah.

quiz.q: Why do the Samaritans finally believe in Jesus?

options.text: They hear Him for themselves and know He truly is the Savior of the world.
options.note: Verse 42 shows their faith moving from the woman's testimony to firsthand hearing of Jesus.

options.text: Only because the woman told them about Him.
options.note: Her testimony began it, verse 39, but they say they now believe because they have heard for themselves.

options.text: Because Jesus performed signs among them.
options.note: No sign is recorded in the town; they believe because of His message heard directly.

options.text: Because Jesus promised them political freedom.
options.note: There is no such promise; they confess Him as Savior of the world, not a political liberator.

quiz.q: What marks the faith of the royal official in the second sign?

options.text: He took Jesus at His word that his son would live and departed trusting it.
options.note: Verse 50 shows him believing Jesus' bare word before any evidence.

options.text: He believed only after seeing his son healed with his own eyes.
options.note: He believed the word first and set out; the confirmation came later on the road.

options.text: He trusted Jesus' promise and set out for home believing.
options.note: True, but it omits the striking point that he trusted the bare word before any proof.

options.text: He demanded that Jesus come and touch his son in person.
options.note: He first asked Jesus to come down, but then took Him at His word without His coming.

questions: Jesus crossed barriers of race, gender, and reputation to reach one woman. Who might you be overlooking that Jesus would cross barriers to reach?
Jesus offered water that satisfies forever, yet we keep returning to wells that leave us thirsty. What broken cisterns are you drinking from instead of coming to Him?
Jesus knew everything the woman had ever done and still offered her living water. How does it free you to be fully known by Him and still fully welcomed?
The Father is seeking worshipers who worship in spirit and truth. What would it look like for your worship to depend less on place and mood and more on the Spirit and the truth of Christ?
The official simply took Jesus at His word. Where is Jesus asking you to trust His word before you can see the outcome?

translationNotes.note: The sixth hour; the BSB footnote explains this means about noon, an unusual time to draw water, hinting at the woman's isolation.
The explanatory clause for Jews do not associate with Samaritans; the BSB footnote notes some manuscripts omit it. It captures the deep estrangement Jesus crosses.
Ripe for harvest renders a word the BSB footnote says is literally white; the fields white for harvest picture the ingathering of people to Christ.
I who speak to you am He renders ego eimi, I am, a phrase that throughout John echoes the divine name and reaches its fullest force in the later I am sayings.
